summary: 12Al-20Mn-1C is a Fe–Mn–Al–C lightweight steel (12 wt% Al, 20 wt% Mn, 1 wt% C) of the composition series studied by Mapelli et al. to map the possible austenite decomposition reactions. This sample is the hot-rolled, water-quenched alloy (from vacuum-induction casting and 1150 °C hot rolling) subsequently tempered at 800 °C for 30 min and water quenched. The 800 °C temper produced full austenitic decomposition through cellular transformation (κ-carbide + α + residual-γ lamellae) combined with spinodal decomposition, with a measured Vickers macro-hardness of 404 HV — the largest hardening gain and the highest tempered hardness among the four compositions tempered at 800 °C.
composition: Nominal composition of the alloy is Fe–12Al–20Mn–1C (wt%), i.e. 12 wt% Al, 20 wt% Mn, 1 wt% C, balance Fe. It belongs to the Fe–Mn–Al–C quaternary lightweight-steel family whose tested composition ranges are Al 9–12 wt%, Mn 10/20/30 wt% and C 0.4–1 wt% (Fe balance). Aluminium is the density-reducing element and also the κ-carbide former, providing the Al–C chemical driving force for κ-carbide precipitation; Mn and C are austenite stabilizers added to improve microstructure and mechanical properties. In this composition the Mn-driven γ-stabilization is balanced by the Al–C driving force for κ-carbide formation, which together govern the decomposition behaviour. EDS of the 800 °C tempered state (Table 7, wt%) shows Al partitioning δ 11.0–13.6 (mean 11.9), γ 5.7–9.9 (mean 7.8) and κ 10.3–11.9 (mean 10.8), and Mn partitioning δ 15.2–20.8 (mean 17.9), γ 20.3–27.6 (mean 23.6) and κ 21.9–25.5 (mean 23.9) — Al is concentrated in δ-ferrite and depleted in γ, while Mn is lowest in δ and highest in γ and κ.
processing: Process genealogy: melting/casting → hot rolling (parent process proc_hot-rolled-1150c) → tempering (this process). (1) The alloy was produced by casting in a 100 kW vacuum induction furnace under vacuum, yielding 0.5 kg ingots. (2) The ingots were hot-rolled at 1150 °C to 5 mm flat products, followed by water quenching (this hot-rolled + water-quenched condition is the parent/benchmark state, proc_hot-rolled-1150c). (3) The sample was then heat treated (tempered) at 800 °C for 30 min, followed by water quenching. Of the two tempering temperatures used in the study (600 °C and 800 °C, both 30 min + water quenching), only the 800 °C treatment triggered cellular transformation and/or spinodal decomposition; 600 °C produced only slight/incipient reactions. The 800 °C tempering supplies fast reaction kinetics, enabling strong, widespread transformations even during the short 30 min hold.
microstructure: The 800 °C tempered 12Al-20Mn-1C underwent full austenitic decomposition, sharing features with the 9Al-10Mn-1C alloy (Figs. 5(a) and 6) but distinguished by the morphology of its κ-carbides. γ grains decomposed by cellular transformation into κ-carbide + α-ferrite + residual-γ lamellar structures, together with spinodal decomposition of γ. In this composition the Mn-induced γ-stabilization was balanced by the Al–C driving force for κ-carbide formation. The κ-carbides of the cellular product consist of wide, thick lath-like lamellae, visibly wider and thicker than at 9% Al (Fig. 7); the laths occur in several orientations with small dark elongated pits inside, and the inter-lamellar spacing is high. Optical metallography (Fig. 5(c)) shows dark, elongated stringers/bands lying in a lighter matrix, banded along the rolling direction. Alongside the cellular product, spinodal decomposition formed nano-sized κ-carbides with a proper cuboidal morphology — the densest and thickest configuration among the three compositions examined (Fig. 8(c),(d)), arranged as an orthogonal checkerboard grid and, in places, separated into differently oriented regions by a boundary. Some grains show a mixed structure in which δ-ferrite branches (linked to δ + κ-carbide lamellar grains) extend inside spinodal decomposed γ grains, whose matrix carries a fine periodic cross-hatched modulation (Fig. 14). Phase constituents identified are κ-carbide (ordered fcc-based E2₁/L1₂, KAPPA_E21), α-ferrite (BCC_A2), residual austenite (FCC_A1) and δ-ferrite (BCC_A2); interfaces include κ/γ, α/κ and δ-ferrite/spinodal-decomposed-γ. Phase fractions and grain sizes are not reported.
properties: Vickers macro-hardness of the 800 °C tempered 12Al-20Mn-1C (5 kg load, 5 indentations per sample): 404 HV. This compares with 357 HV in the parent hot-rolled + water-quenched state (proc_hot-rolled-1150c), i.e. a hardening gain of +47 HV. Among the four compositions tempered at 800 °C, this alloy showed both the largest hardness gain (9Al-10Mn-1C 273→356, 12Al-10Mn-1C 401→399, 12Al-20Mn-1C 357→404, 12Al-30Mn-1C 324→352 HV) and the highest tempered hardness (404 HV). Hardening is attributed to the fully decomposed microstructure (cellular κ + α + residual-γ lamellae plus cuboidal nano-κ from spinodal decomposition), and the observed hardening is consistent despite the high inter-lamellar spacing. No tensile, ductility, physical, chemical or corrosion data are reported for this sample. Characterization techniques applied across the study and to this material: optical microscopy (through-thickness embedding, grinding, polishing); scanning electron microscopy in secondary-electron (SEI) and back-scattered-electron (BSE) modes with EDS/EDX for qualitative local phase composition (Table 7 for the δ, γ and κ phases); and Vickers macro-hardness testing (5 kg load, 5 indentations per sample), with Minitab18 used for data consistency checks and CALPHAD phase-fraction diagrams supporting the thermodynamic interpretation.
mechanisms: Tempering at 800 °C supplies the maximum acceleration of reaction kinetics (thermal energy input), so strong and widespread austenite transformations proceed even within the short 30 min hold.

The Al–C chemical driving force for κ-carbide formation balances the Mn-induced stabilization of austenite in 12Al-20Mn-1C; when this balance tips, the austenite becomes unstable and decomposes, so decomposition is set jointly by composition (driving force and phase equilibria) and tempering temperature (kinetics).

Cellular transformation is an eutectoid-type reaction featuring grain-boundary migration: γ → κ-carbide + α-ferrite + residual-γ lamellar structure; residual γ is detected within the κ-carbide lamellae, indicating an incomplete reaction.

Spinodal decomposition of austenite proceeds as γ → γ0 + γ′ → γ0 + L1₂ → γ0 + L1₂/E2₁: Al and C enrichment/depletion of the γ phase creates carbon-rich and carbon-lean regions, the carbon-enriched region develops short-range-ordered SRO-L1₂ (Al at cube corners, Fe/Mn at faces), and further C ordering at the octahedral sites produces E2₁, giving nano-sized cuboidal κ-carbides.

Increasing Al content to 12 wt% enlarges the thermodynamic gradient in austenite stability between the hot-rolling (1150 °C) and tempering equilibria: the fcc field lines shift toward higher temperatures and away from the tempering temperature, so austenite is destabilized and its propensity to transform during tempering is raised relative to the 9Al grades.

Because austenite stability rises with Mn content, spinodal decomposition becomes more significant and occurs at the expense of cellular transformation; spinodal decomposition requires fast reaction kinetics and a fair balance between austenite stability and the Al–C chemical driving force.

The wide, thick lath-like κ-carbide lamellae and their high inter-lamellar spacing set the hardness response of this composition; the alloy nevertheless hardens because spinodal decomposition contributes its dense, thick cuboidal nano-κ precipitates.
The thick precipitates formed by spinodal decomposition are associated in the literature with brittleness, so a hardness increase of this type may not translate into improved ductility.
The mixed structure in which δ-ferrite branches (linked to δ + κ-carbide lamellar grains) penetrate spinodal decomposed γ grains is reported as an unexplained phenomenon requiring further study.
conclusions: For high Al and C with medium Mn (12Al-20Mn-1C), tempering at 800 °C produced both spinodal decomposition and cellular transformation, giving full austenitic decomposition into widespread κ + α + residual-γ lamellar structures (from cellular transformation), scattered spinodal decomposed γ, and thin band-shaped δ-ferrite/δ + κ-carbide features. The resulting κ-carbides are wide, thick lath-like lamellae, wider and thicker than at 9% Al, and the nano-sized spinodal κ-carbides adopt the densest, thickest cuboidal morphology of the alloys studied. This microstructure raised hardness from 357 HV (hot-rolled) to 404 HV — the largest gain and the highest tempered hardness among the four compositions tempered at 800 °C — even though the inter-lamellar spacing is high. In the broader series, only the 800 °C tempered alloys underwent cellular transformation and/or spinodal decomposition, whereas 600 °C caused only slight/incipient reactions (discontinuous precipitation and precipitation transformation). Within the 12Al group, 12Al-10Mn-1C fully cellular-transformed into coarse α + κ lamellae with high inter-lamellar spacing, which did not improve hardness; the best combination in the study was judged to be 9Al-10Mn-1C at 600 °C, whose discontinuous-precipitation κ-carbides have narrow inter-lamellar spacing, giving the highest hardness and, per the literature, better tensile ductility. The paper concludes that the type of austenite reaction is governed by chemical-composition driving force, thermal energy input and austenite thermodynamic stability, and notes that further work is needed to understand the δ-ferrite branch morphology and the proposed wider hardening routes.
unmapped: Benchmark context: the parent hot-rolled + water-quenched state of this alloy had a Vickers hardness of 357 HV, and the improvement on 800 °C tempering is +47 HV.
